summary: Describes the format of an LDAP URL, which spells out an LDAP search to fetch information from a directory, or points to a service where an operation can continue, such as in a referral. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A web link that holds a question for the address book, so clicking it runs the search.

questions: what is a critical extension in an ldap url
subtitle: How to write an LDAP search, or a pointer to an LDAP server, as a single URL.

tldr.problem: An LDAP directory search has several parts (server, entry name, attributes, scope, filter), and people and programs need a compact way to write one down, for example in a referral to another server.
tldr.mechanism: An LDAP URL starts with ldap:// and packs the host, port, distinguished name, attribute list, scope, filter and optional extensions into one string, using percent-encoding for special characters and fixed defaults for omitted parts.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 2255 and is part of the LDAP technical specification. Clients must take care with security policy when following such URLs.

today: RFC 4516 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2255. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4516 specifies the LDAP URL format for version 3 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). An LDAP URL describes a search operation that retrieves information from a directory. In the context of an LDAP referral or reference, it instead describes a service where an operation can be carried on.

Not every parameter of an LDAP search operation can be expressed in this format. URLs may also stand for reference knowledge, including for non-search operations. The RFC also defines an extension mechanism so the URL can later give access to new LDAP extensions, and it replaces RFC 2255.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of describing a whole question out loud, you write it as one line, like a web link. Sometimes the link just says which office to go to next.

sections.title: The URL Grammar
sections.content:
An LDAP URL begins with the scheme ldap. The grammar is written in ABNF and has these pieces in order: host and optional port, then a slash and a dn, then up to four more parts separated by question marks: attributes, scope, filter and extensions.

  • dn: an LDAP Distinguished Name in the string format of RFC 4514. It is the base object of a search or the target of a non-search operation.
  • attributes: a comma-separated list of the attributes to return.
  • scope: base for a base object search, one for a one-level search or sub for a subtree search.
  • filter: a search filter in the format of RFC 4515.

The host may be a literal IPv6 address as allowed by RFC 3986.
sections.plainLanguage: The link has slots in a fixed order: which computer, which entry, what details you want, how deep to look, and what to match. A question mark separates each slot.

sections.title: Extensions and Critical Extensions
sections.content:
The extensions part is a comma-separated list of type=value pairs, where the value may be left out for extensions that need none. These URL extensions are not necessarily related to any of the LDAP protocol extension mechanisms.

An extension prefixed with ! is critical; one without it is non-critical. If a client implements an extension, it MUST use it. If it does not implement an extension and the extension is critical, it MUST NOT process the URL. If it does not implement a non-critical extension, it MUST ignore it.

The extension type can be a numeric OID such as 1.2.3.4 or a descriptor such as myLDAPURLExtension. Descriptors SHOULD be limited to registered names (see RFC 4520). This RFC defines no extensions itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can carry extra instructions. If the instruction has a bang in front, it is a must-follow: a program that does not understand it has to stop. Without the bang, the program may skip it.

sections.title: Percent-Encoding
sections.content:
A generated LDAP URL MUST use only characters from the reserved, unreserved and pct-encoded productions of RFC 3986. Implementations SHOULD accept other valid UTF-8 strings as input.

An octet MUST be percent-encoded when it is outside the reserved and unreserved sets, when it is the reserved character ? inside a dn, filter or other element, and when it is a comma inside an extension value. Only the extensions component may contain null (zero) bytes before encoding.

Two layers of escaping can meet. A filter escapes null bytes with a backslash, as in (four-octet=\00\00\00\04), and because the backslash must itself be escaped in a URL it becomes %5c.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters have special jobs in a link, like the question mark. To use one as plain text, you swap it for a percent sign and a code, like a secret handshake.

sections.title: Defaults for Omitted Fields
sections.content:
When a field is absent and nothing else says otherwise, these defaults SHOULD be used. Other documents MAY give different rules; RFC 4511, for example, has its own rule for the DN of a URL returned as a referral.

  • host: the client needs prior knowledge of a suitable server.
  • port: TCP port 389.
  • dn: the zero-length DN.
  • attributes: all user attributes, for example via the star selector.
  • scope: base.
  • filter: (objectClass=*).
  • extensions: none.
sections.plainLanguage: If you leave a slot empty, the computer fills in a sensible guess: look only at the named entry, and show everything about it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a series of examples. ldap:///o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US is a base object search of that entry, on a server of the client's choosing, requesting all attributes. Adding a host such as ldap1.example.net names the server. A trailing ?postalAddress requests only that attribute.

Another example uses port 6666 and ??sub?(cn=Babs%20Jensen) to do a subtree search for a common name. The DN o=Question%3f,c=US shows the encoding of a question mark, and o=An%20Example%5C2C%20Inc.,c=US decodes to o=An Example\2C Inc.,c=US.

The URLs ldap://ldap.example.net, ldap://ldap.example.net/ and ldap://ldap.example.net/? are equivalent and point to the root DSE of that server.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same question written shorter or longer, depending on how many slots you fill in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general URL security considerations of RFC 3986 apply. Because URLs are likely to be processed automatically, clients may meet many different servers. A client SHOULD have a user-configurable policy about which servers it will open LDAP sessions with and with which security mechanisms, and SHOULD NOT open sessions that break that policy. If it reuses an existing session, it MUST ensure the session fits the URL and violates no policy.

Absent a policy that permits sending authentication information, a client should use an anonymous session. Reusable passwords should not be used in URL processing unless policy explicitly permits it, and for a referral for an update operation, strong authentication methods SHOULD be used. Following a URL may also cause unexpected results, such as retrieving large amounts of data or starting a long-lived search.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can send your computer to a stranger's server. So the program should follow your rules, and not hand over secrets unless you allowed it.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2255
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the changes from RFC 2255. Technical changes include moving the ABNF to common productions, referring to RFC 3986 in place of RFC 2396 (which allows literal IPv6 addresses in the host), and allowing a star in the attribute list. The extension type became an OID, and the earlier bindname extension was removed for lack of known implementations.

The text on handling implemented and unimplemented extensions was also strengthened, to closely match the approach of RFC 4511 for LDAP controls.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the changelog: the newer version tidies the rules, allows newer address styles and drops one rarely used feature.
